Neonates of the Eastern coral snake (Micrurus corallinus) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after a protracted incubation period; under controlled conditions maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the eggs hatch following approximately 85.5 days [ab = approximately 85.5 days] at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], a duration that falls comfortably within the broader range of 78 to 93 days observed in related elapids. These hatchlings exhibit a snout-vent length at birth of 18.7 centimeters [Lb = 18.7 centimeters], corresponding to a total length of roughly 177 to 197 millimeters, and they carry a modest neonatal body mass averaging 2.39 grams [Wwb = 2.39 grams], though individual variation spans a range of 2.02 to 2.76 grams. This combination of a relatively small birth size and moderate incubation period is consistent with the reproductive strategy of many fossorial or semi-fossorial snakes, where clutch sizes are often limited by maternal body cavity volume and the energetic constraints of producing large, yolk-rich ova. The newly emerged individuals are immediately capable of independent movement and begin searching for suitable microhabitats, although they remain entirely reliant on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching.

As these juveniles grow, they undergo significant morphological changes, progressing through the stage of a young-of-year reptile before reaching sexual maturation. Females attain reproductive maturity once they achieve a total length at puberty of 42.5 centimeters [Lp = 42.5 centimeters], whereas males reach puberty at a slightly greater length of 44 centimeters [Lp = 44 centimeters]; this reversed sexual size dimorphism is uncommon among snakes and warrants further investigation into the hormonal and ecological drivers of maturation in this species. In terms of ultimate size, females are considerably larger than males, reaching an ultimate total length of 95 centimeters [Li = 95 centimeters], while male conspecifics max out at a more modest 74 centimeters [Li = 74 centimeters]. This pronounced female-biased size dimorphism is hypothesized to result from fecundity selection, wherein larger body size in females permits the production of larger clutches, a pattern well-documented across numerous oviparous snake lineages. The growth trajectory from the initial 18.7 centimeters snout-vent length to these adult maxima is gradual and likely influenced by prey availability and local thermal conditions.

Reproductive output in Micrurus corallinus has been quantified under laboratory conditions that closely mimic the thermal regime of its subtropical habitat. When maintained at a constant temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], gravid females produce clutches ranging from 2 to 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 12 eggs per clutch], and they typically achieve a reproductive frequency of approximately 1.2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.2 clutches per year]. This combination yields a moderate annual reproductive rate that balances the energetic demands of egg production against the constraints of a relatively elongated incubation period. Interestingly, the daily reproduction rate inferred from these values underscores the species' conservative breeding strategy, which may be an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of small vertebrate prey in its forest-floor habitat. The reported values are consistent with those documented in other New World coral snakes, though direct comparisons remain limited due to the scarcity of long-term field studies on this elusive species.

Body mass scaling relationships provide additional insight into the species' life history. For comparative purposes, researchers have recorded that individuals of Micrurus corallinus attain a wet weight of 30.1 grams  at a snout-vent length of 55.1 centimeters, and a slightly greater mass of 33.3 grams  at a snout-vent length of 59.6 centimeters. These data points, though derived from a congeneric species, offer a useful benchmark for evaluating the condition of Micrurus corallinus individuals encountered during field surveys. In Eastern coral snakes, body condition indices are strongly correlated with prey abundance, and individuals in poorer condition are more frequently observed during prolonged dry spells when their preferred prey of small lizards and snakes becomes scarce. The rapid growth phase from juvenile to adult is particularly energy-intensive, and suboptimal foraging conditions during this period can delay the onset of puberty and reduce overall lifetime reproductive output.

Longevity records for Micrurus corallinus are scarce, but maximum lifespan has been estimated by extrapolation from data on the closely related harlequin coral snake (Micrurus fulvius). Under captive conditions maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum life span of Micrurus corallinus is approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years], a value extrapolated from data on the closely related Micrurus fulvius, and it is reasonable to assume that this species possesses a similar potential longevity given its comparable body size and ecological niche. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturity and moderate reproductive output, places the Eastern coral snake within the slow end of the life-history continuum for snakes, where individuals invest heavily in survival at the expense of early and prolific reproduction. Field-based mark-recapture studies are urgently needed to confirm these estimates and to explore how environmental gradients in temperature and precipitation might modulate senescence rates and age-specific mortality schedules across the species' geographic range.
